Function approximation: share a value, share an error

A worked feature update explains generalization, aliasing, semi-gradients and moving targets.

Suppose a sensor reports a position you have never visited. A separate table row has learned nothing there, even if you have observed nearby states. Can one observation teach us about those states too? Function approximation lets states share a prediction rule. We will calculate one shared update, see a distinction the rule cannot represent, and then work through how an update can change the successor's prediction and move the training target. Sutton and Barto, Chapter 9.

Part 3. Previously: bootstrapping.

Reading goal: see how one example changes predictions at two states, calculate what the model cannot represent, and follow how fitting the current target changes the next one.

The table growsOne update shares learningSharing can erase distinctionsHold the target stillThe target moves next timeNetworks need steadier targets

The table grows

A Q table stores one number for each state and action. That works for a small grid. With continuous sensor readings, we first have to decide which observations should share a row.

To count the entries, use ddd for the number of sensor dimensions, bbb for the number of bins per dimension, and aaa for the number of available actions. The full Q table has NNN entries, where bdb^dbd counts all combinations of the ddd binned sensor readings. Here aaa counts actions; in the previous episode, it stood for a particular action:

N=a bd.N=a\,b^d. N=abd.

Consider an illustrative cart-balancing task with four sensors: position, speed, pole angle and angular speed. Six bins per sensor give us 1,296 state rows. With two actions, that means 2,592 Q entries. Increasing to twelve bins per sensor gives us 20,736 rows and 41,472 entries.

Doubling the resolution in four dimensions gives us sixteen times as many rows. We need observations to train those rows too, because the table learns each one separately. So memory is only part of the problem. Coarser bins let states within a bin share a prediction, but predictions jump at bin boundaries.

With function approximation, a compact rule can use one observation to update predictions across several states, without waiting for each state to receive its own data. This is the generalization problem described in Sutton and Barto, Part II and Section 9.1.

One update shares learning

How can one example change predictions at several states? In a table, a new row starts empty even if we just trained on a similar state. We can reuse that example by making both states' predictions depend on the same adjustable numbers.

For a state-value example, we can store a few weights instead of a separate value for every state. Here sss is a state, x(s)x(s)x(s) is its fixed vector of numerical features, and www is a weight vector with the same length. The superscript ⊤\top⊤ turns a column vector into a row, so w⊤x(s)w^\top x(s)w⊤x(s) multiplies the corresponding coordinates and adds the results. We write the approximate state value as v^(s,w)\hat v(s,w)v^(s,w); the hat marks an estimate. An assignment arrow in an update replaces the old weights. Our prediction rule is

v^(s,w)=w⊤x(s).\hat v(s,w)=w^\top x(s). v^(s,w)=w⊤x(s).

Take two states, A and B, with features x(A)=(1,1)⊤x(\mathrm A)=(1,1)^\topx(A)=(1,1)⊤ and x(B)=(1,2)⊤x(\mathrm B)=(1,2)^\topx(B)=(1,2)⊤. With initial weights w=(0,0)⊤w=(0,0)^\topw=(0,0)⊤, both predictions are zero. Suppose we are given a training target yyy of 2 at A and use α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1 as the step size. The linear squared-error update is

w←w+α[y−v^(A,w)]x(A).w\leftarrow w+\alpha[y-\hat v(\mathrm A,w)]x(\mathrm A). w←w+α[y−v^(A,w)]x(A).

The error is 2, so both weights become 0.2. A now predicts 0.4 and B predicts 0.6, even though we have given the model no example from B. If B's target is 3, its prediction has moved closer too.

After training only A once A: features (1, 1) B: features (1, 2)
Before 0 0
After 0.4 0.6
Supplied comparison target 2 3

Both predictions change because each weight affects every input that uses its feature. The update moves in a direction that locally reduces A's squared error. Whether it also helps B depends on B's features and target. Sutton and Barto, Sections 9.3–9.4.

Describe the visited state with its feature vector.
Compute target minus prediction.
Add step size × error × features to the weights.
Recompute any state's value with the new weights.

Sharing can erase distinctions

But what if two states need different predictions and we give them identical features? More training cannot recover a distinction we removed from the representation.

Call these states C and D. The names are labels, rather than variables. We use the same www and feature rule as before. Suppose their true values are 0 and 2, but both have the feature vector (1,0)⊤(1,0)^\top(1,0)⊤. If ccc is the first weight, every possible setting of the weights gives

v^(C,w)=v^(D,w)=c.\hat v(\mathrm C,w)=\hat v(\mathrm D,w)=c. v^(C,w)=v^(D,w)=c.

If we see examples from both states equally often and fit with squared error, the best shared prediction is the mean of their values:

c=0+22=1.c=\frac{0+2}{2}=1. c=20+2​=1.

That leaves both states with an error of 1. We call this aliasing: the states differ, but the value function sees them as the same. If we sampled one state more often, the shared estimate would move toward that state's target. Sutton and Barto, Sections 9.1–9.3.

A coarse sensor bin can cause this problem. In the cart-balancing example, two pole positions may look similar while their angular speeds imply very different futures. If the representation records only the angle, it loses that distinction.

Check whether conflicting examples have identical features.
If so, add the missing predictive information.
Refit using features that distinguish the two states.

Giving the states different feature vectors allows different predictions. Adding parameters can help only if the inputs still contain the relevant information.

Hold the target still

So far, we have supplied the training target. Now suppose we use the model's prediction at a successor to build it. The model predicts 0.4 at the current state and 0.6 at its successor. With a reward of 0 and a discount of 0.9, the target is 0.54. We can fit 0.4 toward that number, but differentiating through the calculation that produced 0.54 gives a different update. Semi-gradient TD holds 0.54 fixed while taking this derivative.

Here ttt counts transitions, StS_tSt​ is the current state, and Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ is the reward received after action AtA_tAt​. We use wtw_twt​ for the current weights and γ\gammaγ for the discount, between 0 and 1. We calculate the one-step target yty_tyt​ with those weights, taking the terminal value to be zero:

yt=Rt+1+γv^(St+1,wt).y_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma\hat v(S_{t+1},w_t). yt​=Rt+1​+γv^(St+1​,wt​).

For this update, we treat yty_tyt​ as a fixed number. We write the squared error against it as Lt(w)L_t(w)Lt​(w). The symbol ∇w\nabla_w∇w​ means the vector of derivatives with respect to the weights:

Lt(w)=12[yt−v^(St,w)]2.L_t(w)=\tfrac12[y_t-\hat v(S_t,w)]^2. Lt​(w)=21​[yt​−v^(St​,w)]2.

The weights after this transition are wt+1w_{t+1}wt+1​, and α\alphaα is still the step size. Writing δt=yt−v^(St,wt)\delta_t=y_t-\hat v(S_t,w_t)δt​=yt​−v^(St​,wt​) for the TD error, the update is

wt+1=wt+αδt∇wv^(St,wt).w_{t+1}=w_t+\alpha\delta_t\nabla_w\hat v(S_t,w_t). wt+1​=wt​+αδt​∇w​v^(St​,wt​).

With linear features, the gradient is x(St)x(S_t)x(St​). This is semi-gradient TD: we differentiate through the prediction we are fitting while ignoring how the target depends on the weights. Sutton and Barto, Sections 9.3–9.4.

Compute the target with the current weights.
Detach that number from differentiation.
Differentiate the current state's prediction.
Update weights; recompute the next target next time.

This step moves the current prediction toward the target we just calculated. Later targets are recomputed, so this local fitting direction is different from minimizing one fixed loss throughout training.

The target moves next time

Holding the target constant during differentiation does not keep future targets fixed. With shared weights, an update changes both sides of the next TD error.

Let's return to A and B with their earlier features and weights (0.2,0.2)⊤(0.2,0.2)^\top(0.2,0.2)⊤, and take a transition from A to B. Use a reward of zero, a discount of 0.9 and a step size of 0.1. A predicts 0.4 and B predicts 0.6, so the target is 0.54 and the TD error is 0.14. Here wt+1w_{t+1}wt+1​ is the updated weight vector, and yt+1y_{t+1}yt+1​ below means the target on the next replay of this same stored transition:

wt+1=(0.2,0.2)⊤+0.1(0.14)(1,1)⊤=(0.214,0.214)⊤.w_{t+1}=(0.2,0.2)^\top+0.1(0.14)(1,1)^\top =(0.214,0.214)^\top. wt+1​=(0.2,0.2)⊤+0.1(0.14)(1,1)⊤=(0.214,0.214)⊤.

With the new weights, A predicts 0.428 and B predicts 0.642. If we train on the same transition again, the target becomes

yt+1=0+0.9(0.642)=0.5778.y_{t+1}=0+0.9(0.642)=0.5778. yt+1​=0+0.9(0.642)=0.5778.

Same replayed A → B transition Before After one update
Prediction at A 0.4 0.428
Prediction at B 0.6 0.642
Target from B 0.54 0.5778

The target has increased from 0.54 to 0.5778 because the update also raised B's value. With a table, updating A would have left B's separate entry unchanged.

Fit the current target once.
Recompute the successor's prediction.
Compare the new target with the previous target.

This calculation shows how the predictions are coupled; it does not prove divergence. Linear TD prediction has convergence results for a fixed policy with on-policy sampling and appropriate technical conditions. Other sampling distributions can break that stability. Sutton and Barto, Sections 9.4 and 11.2.

Networks need steadier targets

A neural network can learn intermediate features along with its output weights, where a linear predictor is limited by the features we design for it. But the network still shares parameters across inputs, so it has the same coupling problem.

For action values, we write Qθ(s,a)Q_\theta(s,a)Qθ​(s,a) for the network's estimate for taking action aaa in state sss, using learned parameters θ\thetaθ. To build targets, we keep a separate target-network copy with parameters θˉ\bar\thetaθˉ, held fixed between scheduled refreshes. Here a′a'a′ ranges over actions available at the next state, and max⁡a′\max_{a'}maxa′​ selects the largest prediction among them. The observed reward is Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ and the successor is St+1S_{t+1}St+1​. DQN calculates the target ztz_tzt​ as

zt=Rt+1+γmax⁡a′Qθˉ(St+1,a′).z_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_{\bar\theta}(S_{t+1},a'). zt​=Rt+1​+γa′max​Qθˉ​(St+1​,a′).

When the transition terminates, the target is just the reward. Otherwise, it includes the largest next-action estimate selected by the max. The learned network fits the resulting number while the target copy remains fixed.

Save transitions in replay memory.
Sample a batch of saved transitions.
Build targets with the frozen copy; fit the live network.
Periodically copy the live parameters to the target copy.

Replay lets us reuse observations and break up consecutive samples. The separate network copy slows changes in the estimated tail of the return. These are the mechanisms used by Mnih et al., DQN, 2015.

Sharing buys:

  • Compact storage. Parameters replace separate entries for every possible input.
  • Transfer. One example can improve predictions at related states.
  • Flexible features. Networks can learn useful representations from observations.

Costs and conditions:

  • Representation error. Identical features force identical predictions.
  • Interference. An update can worsen predictions elsewhere.
  • Stability. Replay and target copies help training; they provide no general convergence guarantee for neural Q-learning.

Which policy produced those transitions, and which policy does their target evaluate? Part 4: on-policy and off-policy learning explains the distinction. We return to the stability problem in Part 5.
